newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: China pre-festive demand seen propping oil prices.
newsitem.headline: China pre-festive demand seen propping oil prices.

text.p: China's pre-festive season demand for oil products is soaring as buyers stock up for a cold winter and is expected to keep prices buoyant, industry sources said on Tuesday.
China has begun a buying spree for liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), diesel and fuel oil ahead of the one week-long Chinese Lunar New Year holidays in early February.
Chinese importers told Reuters the stockpiling of oil products was essential to tide over a week of celebrations when trading activities will come to standstill.
The sources said China's imports of oil products this year were expected to surpass those in the same period last year because domestic inventories were at lower than normal levels.
Industry experts estimated that China already had imported around 800,000 tonnes of fuel oil in November and December and was expected to import at least 300,000 tonnes more in January.
Sources said LPG imports would be double those in the same period last year, totalling more than 600,000 tonnes in November and December.
Already, China has imported more than 1.3 million tonnes of diesel since November, compared with a total of 1.1 million tonnes in November and December last year.
Chinese traders said they were taking advantage of the softer gas oil price after levels fell from a five-year peak of $34.15 per barrel on December 6 to $32 on December 16.
"Previous high gas oil prices kept buyers away from the spot market and domestic inventories were gradually being depleted," said a source from state trader Sinochem in Singapore.
Gas oil, which is China main transport fuel, makes up more than 60 percent of oil product imports to China.

"Besides having to stock-pile for the Chinese new year holidays, China's import of fuel oil and gas oil usually increases near the end of the year as more fuel is needed to run power stations during the winter," a trader in Sinochem Hong Kong told Reuters.
"More LPG will also be required as there will be a lot of cooking to celebrate the Lunar New Year."
Industry sources said China was still buying and imports would only come to a temporary halt in mid-January.

China's increased imports of fuel oil have already kept prices buoyant, traders said. Prices nudged 50 cents higher last week and were $120 per tonne on Monday. Singapore traders said they expected prices to rise as Chinese demand remained strong.
Soaring LPG prices did not dampen Chinese buying. Asian LPG prices soared to the highest level in a decade at $310 per tonne in early December, up more than US$100 from a year ago.
"Despite the soaring prices, we still have to import as domestic output is insufficent to meet demand," said an LPG trader.
Chinese traders were also seen to be active lately in the swaps market as many hedged their risks as they bought more cargoes on a floating price basis, traders in Singapore said.
"They were the main feature player the whole of last week," said one broker.
